summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which carries the federal Penal Code offences, the identity-document rules and the entry position; those apply here as they do nationwide and are set out in the national record. The state's own layer is its Sharia criminal law.

In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 (Negeri Sembilan), which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power; those rulings concern other states, not Negeri Sembilan's section 66.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia through interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric.

Enforcement against trans and gender-nonconforming people in Negeri Sembilan is carried out by the state Islamic religious department under Sharia provisions that apply to Muslims. The Human Dignity Trust profile of Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records a national crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, alongside the persistence of federal criminalisation under Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936, which carry up to 20 years' imprisonment with whipping.
tangentialFactors:
The Court of Appeal's 2014 ruling on section 66 was a federalism and rights decision about a state legislature's power to legislate a cross-dressing offence; it did not decriminalise same-sex conduct under the federal Penal Code, which continues to apply in Negeri Sembilan as nationwide.

The Federal Court's later decisions striking down Sharia provisions in Selangor and Kelantan rest on the same federalism reasoning that state legislatures lack criminal-law power over those subjects. Whether comparable provisions in Negeri Sembilan's own enactments would survive a similar challenge is not addressed in these sources.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters interviews covered 2018 to 2021, so the conditions they describe reflect that period rather than a current survey of Negeri Sembilan.
localsOnly:
Section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992, which had criminalised cross-dressing in Negeri Sembilan, was declared unconstitutional by the Court of Appeal in November 2014 and no longer operates as a valid state offence.

Muslim residents of Negeri Sembilan remain subject to the state's other Sharia provisions and to the state Islamic religious department's enforcement powers, as well as to federal Penal Code provisions that apply to everyone.

People living in Negeri Sembilan were among those interviewed by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters for their August 2022 report on state-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, covering interviews conducted between 2018 and 2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any replacement or renumbered cross-dressing provision was enacted in Negeri Sembilan after the 2014 judgment is not stated in these sources.

The sources do not document specific enforcement incidents, raids or arrests against trans people within Negeri Sembilan itself; the documented raid and arrest record in this inventory concerns Kuala Lumpur, Penang and other states.

No Negeri Sembilan-specific figures for violence against trans people, health-care access, or document-marker decisions appear in this inventory; those matters are carried at the national level.
